> **AWS API Management Platform Guidance** — Composition guidance for building a governed AWS API Management platform: managed gateway ingress combined with centralized identity, policy enforcement, observability, and API lifecycle workflows. Implements the strategy defined in the [Enterprise API and Microservices Strategy](../../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-api-microservices-strategy.md) and composes with [REF-APP-API-001](../../../reference/application/REF-APP-API-001-aws-api-management-reference-architecture.md) and [GUID-APP-IMPL-009](./GUID-APP-IMPL-009-aws-api-management-implementation-guidance.md).

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

Teams implementing APIs on AWS often converge on gateway runtime concerns but diverge on lifecycle governance, consumer onboarding, and shared controls, which creates inconsistent implementation quality. This guidance describes an AWS API Management platform composition that combines managed gateway ingress with centralized identity, policy enforcement, observability, and API lifecycle workflows, so that domain teams onboard APIs against a consistent, governed baseline instead of building these capabilities independently.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#scope-north-south-and-east-west]

#### Scope: North-South and East-West

This guidance primarily addresses **North-South (external-facing) API management** — the ingress layer where consumers outside the service cluster or VPC call domain APIs through the managed gateway.

For **East-West (internal service-to-service) communication**, the active AWS security control baseline — [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB](../../security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB.md) (REQ-APIGW-01, REQ-APIGW-03, REQ-APIGW-04; Pattern B: Internal East-West) — mandates a **Private API Gateway** (endpoint type `PRIVATE`, reachable only via VPC Endpoint) as the control-plane baseline; API Gateway interception is not optional for internal traffic. Apply the following decision framework, gated by that control:

1. **Private API Gateway (mandatory baseline, REST APIs)** — default for all East-West traffic implemented as a REST API; satisfies REQ-APIGW-01/03/04. HTTP and WebSocket APIs do not support the `PRIVATE` endpoint type and support only Regional (internet-routable) endpoints. Per [STD-APP-API-007](../../../../standards/application/api/STD-APP-API-007-aws-api-management-standard-profile.md) Requirement 5 (the authoritative source for this framing), the SBB's control — API Gateway interception plus private, non-internet-routable endpoints — applies to REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs alike, with no exception by API type; because no technical mechanism lets an HTTP or WebSocket API satisfy that control, East-West traffic implemented as an HTTP or WebSocket API is a genuine, unresolved SBB/technical-capability gap, not a design choice this guidance can resolve on its own authority. No internal Application Load Balancer, other private frontend, or VPC Link/NLB integration is authorized as a sanctioned substitute — a VPC Link/NLB integration in particular privatizes only the API Gateway-to-backend integration, not the API's own client-facing endpoint. Re-platform the boundary as a REST API using the `PRIVATE` endpoint type wherever the API's actual requirements permit it; any East-West HTTP or WebSocket API that cannot be re-platformed as REST is an open compliance gap that must be tracked and remediated through Security Architecture's SBB exception process (or an SBB amendment) rather than resolved through a self-approved workaround.
2. **Service mesh (complementary, not substitutive)** — layer [PTN-APP-API-031: Service Mesh Integration Pattern](../../../../patterns/application/api-microservices/PTN-APP-API-031-service-mesh-integration-pattern.md) on top of the Private API Gateway baseline where a domain also needs mTLS, fine-grained service identity, or L7 traffic management (retries, circuit breaking) between services. The mesh augments the identity/transport layer; it does not replace the gateway's interception, authorization, and audit-logging responsibilities.
3. **Hybrid (typical)** — most domain services combine both: Private API Gateway at the East-West REST API boundary, service mesh sidecar for intra-cluster mTLS and traffic shaping.

Use [STD-APP-API-006](../../../../standards/application/api/STD-APP-API-006-api-mesh-vs-gateway-guidance.md) to select among these options for a given API boundary. A domain service may apply this guidance to both boundaries simultaneously: this guidance governs the North-South ingress gateway and the East-West Private API Gateway control point, while the service mesh (where used) governs mTLS and traffic policy for internal calls made by the same service to its upstream dependencies.

Use [GUID-APP-IMPL-010: Enterprise API Engineering Playbook](./GUID-APP-IMPL-010-api-engineering-guidance.md) to determine whether a given API boundary requires this guidance, the service mesh pattern, or both.

### Technical Context

Existing API patterns cover routing, aggregation, and developer portal concepts, but AWS implementation often needs a unifying composition that combines these capabilities in one platform model. The [Enterprise API and Microservices Strategy](../../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-api-microservices-strategy.md) identifies a centralized API management platform as a core component of the enterprise API framework; this guidance is the AWS-specific realization of that requirement.

### Problem Statement

Without a platform composition following this guidance:

- Gateway configurations drift by team and workload.
- API lifecycle controls are inconsistently applied.
- Runtime telemetry and policy evidence are uneven.

**Forces and constraints** that shape the guidance below:

- Need for domain delivery speed.
- Need for platform-level governance consistency.
- Need for security and observability controls aligned with existing guidance.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#trade-offs-and-costs]

### Trade-offs and Costs

Adopting this guidance is not free — teams should weigh the following before applying it:

- **Added gateway hops and latency**: Routing traffic through a managed gateway adds a network hop and policy-evaluation overhead compared to a direct service-to-service call; latency-sensitive APIs must budget for this in their performance objectives.
- **Centralized-platform dependency**: Domain teams depend on the platform team's gateway, identity, and OTel Collector infrastructure being available and correctly configured; an outage or misconfiguration in shared platform components affects every onboarded domain API, not just one team's service.
- **Cost**: Managed gateway, WAF, and Lambda authorizer invocations incur per-request AWS charges that scale with traffic volume; teams with very high request volumes should model this cost before onboarding.
- **Operational complexity**: This guidance introduces additional components to operate and troubleshoot (gateway stages, Lambda authorizers, VPC Links, WAF rules, OTel Collector routing) compared with a simpler direct-call architecture; teams with a small number of low-risk internal APIs may find this overhead disproportionate to the governance benefit.

These trade-offs inform onboarding sequencing, budget planning, and platform capacity decisions — they do not exempt any API from the mandatory Private API Gateway baseline (East-West) or gateway/WAF baseline (North-South) described in Scope.

### Platform Composition

The composition uses a shared AWS API Management platform baseline with domain onboarding waves:

1. Shared platform services provide gateway ingress, identity integration, and baseline controls.
2. Domain APIs onboard using contract and policy validation gates.
3. Runtime telemetry, audit evidence, and lifecycle governance are embedded in release workflows.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#architecture-diagram]

### Architecture Diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Consumer[API Consumer] --> WAF[AWS WAF and Protection Controls]
    WAF --> Gateway[Amazon API Gateway]
    Gateway --> Authorizer[Identity and Authorization Layer]
    Authorizer -->|Deny| Reject[401/403 Response]
    Authorizer -->|Allow policy returned to gateway| GatewayIntegration[API Gateway Integration - performs backend invocation]
    GatewayIntegration --> BackendEKS[Domain Backend - Kubernetes/EKS]
    GatewayIntegration --> BackendServerless[Domain Backend - Lambda/ECS]
    BackendEKS --> OTel[OTel Collector]
    OTel --> Dynatrace[Dynatrace - Enterprise APM]
    BackendServerless --> CWXRay[CloudWatch and X-Ray]
    Gateway --> GWLogs[Gateway Access Logs / Audit]
    GWLogs --> SIEM[Enterprise SIEM]
    Contracts[API Contracts and Policies] --> Pipeline[CI/CD Validation Pipeline]
    Pipeline --> Gateway
```

> **Authorizer scope note:** The Lambda authorizer never invokes the backend directly — it returns an allow/deny IAM policy to API Gateway. On Allow, API Gateway itself (depicted above as the Gateway Integration step) performs the backend invocation; on Deny, API Gateway returns the 401/403 response without ever reaching a backend.

> **Observability Note:** Application services deployed on Kubernetes/EKS should be instrumented with the OpenTelemetry SDK and route telemetry through the OTel Collector per [STD-APP-MON-002](../../../../standards/application/monitoring/STD-APP-MON-002-opentelemetry-observability.md) — proposed, pending that standard's Domain EA and Security Architecture ratification (currently `status: draft`) — which routes to Dynatrace as the primary enterprise APM. Backend services deployed on Lambda or ECS (outside Kubernetes/EKS scope) use CloudWatch and X-Ray as the AWS-native observability backends instead; these are not required to route through OTel. Gateway-level access logs and audit trails are forwarded to enterprise SIEM separate from application telemetry.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#identity-provider-integration]

##### Identity Provider Integration

The enterprise identity provider at Gainwell is **Microsoft Entra ID (Gainwell People Directory / GPD)**, which supports OAuth 2.0 / OIDC natively. Amazon API Gateway integrates with Entra ID via a **Lambda authorizer** that validates Entra ID-issued JWT tokens directly against the GPD JWKS endpoint — no intermediate identity broker (e.g., Amazon Cognito) is required.

- For **workforce and internal API consumers**, the Lambda authorizer validates Entra ID JWT tokens using the GPD JWKS endpoint. Platform Engineering maintains the authorizer and trust configuration.
- For **IAM-based downstream authorization** (where AWS service calls require scoped AWS credentials), IAM roles with appropriate trust policies are used.
- For **external partner or B2B APIs**, coordinate with Identity Architecture to determine whether federation through GPD or a separate external IdP configuration applies.

> ⚠️ **Citizen-Facing and PHI-Adjacent APIs:** For APIs that serve citizen/member populations or process PHI (e.g., Medicaid portals, member health data), the **enterprise Identity Broker ([GUID-SEC-IAM-IDENTITY-BROKER-2.2.02](../../security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-IDENTITY-BROKER-2.2.02.md))** is the mandated identity mediation layer per the enterprise IAM strategy. **Coordinate with Identity Architecture before selecting an authorization model for these scenarios.**

Platform teams must coordinate with Identity Architecture to select the appropriate integration model during platform foundation. Application teams receive the token issuance endpoint and audience claim values; they do not configure the IdP integration directly.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#pre-backend-request-validation-lambda-authorizers]

##### Pre-Backend Request Validation (Lambda Authorizers)

Before forwarding a request to a backend service, the gateway should enforce authorization and optionally perform custom pre-flight validation. Amazon API Gateway supports two Lambda authorizer types:

| Authorizer Type | Use Case |
| --- | --- |
| **Token authorizer** | Validates a bearer token (JWT or opaque) passed in the `Authorization` header; returns an IAM policy allow/deny |
| **Request authorizer** | Validates request parameters, headers, query strings, or combinations; suitable for API key + context validation or multi-claim policy decisions |

Use Lambda authorizers when:

- Token validation requires custom logic beyond a JWT authorizer (e.g., claims enrichment, OPA policy evaluation).
- Authorization decisions depend on request metadata available to an authorizer — headers, query string parameters, path parameters, or stage variables — not the request body, which Lambda authorizers never receive.
- A third-party IdP token format is not directly supported by the native JWT authorizer.

> **Scope of Lambda authorizers:** API Gateway passes a Lambda authorizer only the method ARN, headers, query string parameters, path parameters, and stage variables — it does not pass the request body. Authorizers therefore cannot perform payload input validation, body normalization, or body-based transformation. Route those concerns to API Gateway request validators (JSON Schema validation on the method request), VTL mapping templates (see [Request/Response Transformation](#requestresponse-transformation-and-protocol-mediation)), or a dedicated integration Lambda placed after the authorizer in the request pipeline.

**TTL and fail-closed requirements:**

- Lambda authorizer response caching **must be configured with `AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds` no greater than 300 seconds for every production API**, per the active AWS security SBB's CON-05 control ([GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB](../../security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB.md) §12.4.6) — this 300-second ceiling applies regardless of the token's own lifetime. For PHI-adjacent or privileged APIs, use the **lower of 300 seconds and the enterprise access token lifetime** (coordinate with Identity Architecture for the applicable bound) — an overly long TTL allows a revoked token or disabled account to continue accessing the API for the full TTL duration.
- **Handled authorizer errors** (the Lambda function completes but token validation or policy evaluation fails) **must return an explicit deny IAM policy (fail closed)** per [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB](../../security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB.md) §12.4.12.
- **Timeout or invocation-failure errors** (the Lambda function times out, throttles, or throws an unhandled exception before returning a policy document) cannot produce a deny policy — the authorizer never completes, so no IAM policy is ever generated. API Gateway itself returns an error response (`500`/`503`) directly to the caller without invoking the backend; this is the fail-closed outcome for this failure class, achieved through the gateway's own default behavior rather than an authorizer-issued deny policy. Failing open (proceeding to backend invocation) on either failure class is prohibited.
- A longer TTL reduces Lambda invocation cost but increases the revocation exposure window — select the lowest TTL that satisfies performance requirements for the API's risk classification.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#endpoint-visibility-private-vs-public]

#### Endpoint Visibility: Private vs. Public

> **Scope: API Gateway REST APIs only.** The three-endpoint-type model below (Regional, Private, Edge-optimized) applies to Amazon API Gateway **REST APIs**. HTTP APIs and WebSocket APIs do not offer this same endpoint-type set — HTTP APIs and WebSocket APIs support only **Regional** endpoints; neither offers a Private (PrivateLink/VPC endpoint) endpoint type or an Edge-optimized (CloudFront) endpoint type. Do not apply the Private-endpoint decision rule below to an HTTP or WebSocket API implementation. For East-West traffic implemented as an HTTP or WebSocket API where the mandatory Private API Gateway baseline (see [Scope: North-South and East-West](#scope-north-south-and-east-west)) cannot be met by a Regional-only endpoint type, a VPC Link/NLB integration is **not** a substitute for a private client-facing endpoint — VPC Link only privatizes the API Gateway-to-backend integration, it does not make the API's own client-facing endpoint non-internet-routable. Per [STD-APP-API-007](../../../../standards/application/api/STD-APP-API-007-aws-api-management-standard-profile.md) Requirement 5 (the authoritative source for this framing), this is a genuine, unresolved SBB/technical-capability gap, not a design choice this guidance can resolve on its own authority: the only currently sanctioned path is to implement that boundary as a REST API using the **Private** (`PRIVATE`) endpoint type; no internal Application Load Balancer, other private frontend, or VPC Link/NLB integration is authorized as a sanctioned substitute. Any East-West HTTP or WebSocket API that cannot be re-platformed as REST is an open compliance gap that must be tracked and remediated through Security Architecture's SBB exception process (or an SBB amendment) rather than resolved through a self-approved workaround.

Amazon API Gateway REST APIs support three endpoint types. Selecting the wrong type has security and cost implications.

| Endpoint Type | Accessibility | When to Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Regional** (default) | Public internet, optionally fronted by CloudFront | External-facing APIs that require global distribution or direct consumer access; WAF association required |
| **Private** | VPC only via VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) | Internal APIs that must never be reachable from the internet; application team–to–platform team communication, internal B2B, or intra-enterprise integration |
| **Edge-optimized** | CloudFront edge network | Geographically distributed external consumers where latency reduction at the edge is the primary driver; less common in enterprise contexts |

**Decision rule (REST APIs):** Default to **Private** endpoints for all REST APIs consumed entirely within the enterprise network. Use **Regional** only when external consumers require direct HTTPS ingress. Private endpoints require a VPC endpoint, but the VPC endpoint's own default policy does not deny access by default — per [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB](../../security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB.md) §153-156, deny-by-default must be implemented explicitly in the API Gateway resource policy; do not rely on the VPC endpoint policy alone for this control.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#transformation]

##### Transformation

Amazon API Gateway supports mapping templates (using Velocity Template Language, VTL) and integration response mappings for lightweight request and response transformation at the gateway tier:

- Use mapping templates to reshape payloads when a backend service contract differs from the published API contract (e.g., field renaming, envelope extraction, injecting context claims into the backend request body).
- Avoid complex transformation logic in VTL; prefer a dedicated adapter or Lambda proxy integration when transformation logic exceeds simple field mapping or when testability is required.
- Document any transformation applied in the OpenAPI spec as an extension (`x-gateway-transform`) to preserve contract traceability.

> ⚠️ **VTL Security:** VTL templates have access to the full request context, including headers, query strings, and authorization claims. Do not embed user-supplied input directly into mapping templates without sanitization — improperly constructed templates can leak authorization context or inject malformed claims into backend requests. Refer to [GUID-SEC-APP-API-SECURITY-2.7.01](../../security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-API-SECURITY-2.7.01.md) §Pattern 3 for the input validation posture required at the gateway tier.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#protocol-mediation]

##### Protocol Mediation

API Gateway REST APIs support HTTP and Lambda proxy integration types. "HTTP integration" here is the AWS API Gateway integration-type name, distinct from the transport protocol — the backend endpoint itself SHALL use HTTPS per Network Security Controls below. Protocol mediation use cases include:

| Scenario | Recommended Approach |
| --- | --- |
| REST to REST (HTTPS backend) | HTTP integration with optional VTL mapping templates; backend endpoint SHALL use HTTPS per Network Security Controls below |
| REST to Lambda | Lambda proxy integration; Lambda performs any internal mediation |
| REST to legacy SOAP/XML backend | Lambda integration as mediator; Lambda translates JSON ↔ XML |
| REST to event backbone (async) | Lambda or SQS integration; gateway returns `202 Accepted` |

Protocol mediation should remain in the gateway or a thin adapter layer and not be embedded in business service logic.
page_texts.30:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#api-key-management-and-multi-tenancy]

#### API Key Management and Multi-Tenancy

Amazon API Gateway API keys combined with usage plans provide a mechanism for consumer identification, rate limiting, and quota enforcement:

- **API Keys** identify calling applications (not users). They are not a replacement for authentication but supplement it for metering and throttling.
- **Usage Plans** associate API keys with throttle and quota policies, enabling per-consumer or per-tier rate limiting.
- **Multi-tenancy models:**

| Model | Description | Appropriate When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single gateway, per-tenant usage plan | All tenants share one gateway; usage plans isolate throttle/quota | Recommended for most enterprise multi-tenant APIs |
| Per-tenant API Key + authorizer-derived tenant routing | The API key identifies the calling application for metering/throttling only; the Lambda/JWT authorizer resolves and validates the tenant claim from the token, injecting a validated tenant context into the request that controlled integration logic (Lambda proxy or a thin routing layer) uses to select the tenant-specific backend. Stage variables are fixed values bound to a deployed stage and cannot be dynamically selected per request by an API key | Tenant-specific backend isolation is required without provisioning a dedicated stage per tenant |
| Per-tenant gateway stage | A dedicated stage — and its own stage variables — provisioned separately for each tenant | Tenant isolation requirements exceed what authorizer-context-based routing can provide |

API keys must be rotated on a defined schedule, stored in an enterprise-approved secrets vault confirmed with Security Architecture (see NHI Note below), and distributed through a secure consumer onboarding workflow (not embedded in client application code or documentation). Where feasible, prefer cryptographically bound, short-lived credentials (mTLS client certificates or OAuth 2.0 workload-identity tokens) over static long-lived API keys, consistent with the active NHI strategy referenced below.

> **NHI Note:** For API keys and credentials consumed programmatically by enterprise services, evaluate requirements against [GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12](../../security/Identity/GUID-SEC-IAM-NON-HUMAN-AND-AI-STRATEGY-2.2.12.md) and its companion [GUID-SEC-IAM-NHI-RAD-2.3.05](../../security/Identity/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-IAM-NHI-RAD-2.3.05.md). Confirm with Security Architecture whether AWS Secrets Manager alone satisfies workload identity credential controls, or whether CyberArk/Conjur is required as the authoritative vault for programmatic credential access.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#vpc-and-network-boundary-controls]

##### VPC and Network Boundary Controls

- All backend services invoked by the gateway must be reachable via VPC-internal networking (private subnets) and must not have public endpoints unless specifically approved through the security architecture exception process.
- Use **VPC Link** for HTTP/HTTPS integrations to route gateway traffic to backend services in a VPC without traversing the public internet.
- Backend service integrations from the API Gateway **SHALL use HTTPS**. HTTP (cleartext) backend integrations are prohibited regardless of whether VPC Link is in use — VPC Link provides network isolation but does not substitute for transport-layer encryption. This requirement aligns with [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB](../../security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-AWS-2.2.04.SSB.md) AD-02 (End-to-End TLS).
- Private API Gateway endpoints require a **VPC endpoint** (Interface endpoint for `execute-api`) with a resource-based policy restricting access to the enterprise VPC(s).
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#ip-allowlisting-and-waf-controls]

##### IP Allowlisting and WAF Controls

- For Regional endpoints, associate an **AWS WAF Web ACL** to restrict inbound access by IP address, geographic region, or rate-based rules.
- Use **resource policies** on the API itself (resource policies attach at the API level, not to an individual stage) to enforce explicit IP allowlisting (CIDR-based) where consumer IP ranges are known and bounded.
- Do not rely on IP allowlisting as the sole access control mechanism; it must supplement authentication and authorization controls, not replace them.
- WAF rules, IP sets, and rate-based rules are platform-owned controls. Application teams specify consumer IP ranges and access patterns during onboarding; the platform team applies the WAF configuration.
page_texts.34:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

- Keep shared controls in platform-owned templates.
- Validate contracts and policies together.
- Require operational readiness evidence before production promotion.
- Default to Private endpoints; require explicit justification for Regional (public) endpoints.
- Use Lambda authorizers for non-standard token validation or pre-backend policy enforcement.
- Route all VPC-internal backend traffic through VPC Link; never expose backends to the public internet.
page_texts.35:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- Implementing gateway routing without lifecycle governance.
- Treating security controls as post-deployment concerns.
- Onboarding domains without telemetry and runbook readiness.
- Using API keys as the sole access control mechanism instead of supplementing authentication.
- Selecting Regional endpoints for internal-only APIs that should use Private endpoints.
- Embedding complex transformation logic in VTL mapping templates instead of a Lambda integration.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#decision-point-1-gateway-tenancy-model]

#### Decision Point 1: Gateway Tenancy Model

**Context:** Selecting how gateway ownership and configuration are segmented across domains.
**Options:** Shared enterprise gateway tenancy; domain-segmented gateway tenancy with shared control templates; hybrid public/private exposure model (see [Variations](#variations)).
**Criteria:** Governance consistency, domain delivery autonomy, and operational complexity (see [Trade-offs and Costs](#trade-offs-and-costs)).
**Recommendation:** Default to shared enterprise gateway tenancy; adopt domain segmentation only where a domain has genuinely distinct isolation or compliance requirements that the shared model cannot satisfy.
page_texts.49:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-011-aws-api-management-platform-guidance.md#decision-point-2-endpoint-visibility-selection]

#### Decision Point 2: Endpoint Visibility Selection

**Context:** Selecting the Amazon API Gateway REST API endpoint type for a given API boundary.
**Options:** Private, Regional, or Edge-optimized (see [Endpoint Visibility: Private vs. Public](#endpoint-visibility-private-vs-public)).
**Criteria:** Whether the API is consumed entirely within the enterprise network or requires direct external HTTPS ingress.
**Recommendation:** Default to Private for all REST APIs consumed entirely within the enterprise network; use Regional only when external consumers require direct HTTPS ingress, per the Endpoint Visibility decision rule.

### Risk Management

| Risk Category | Description | Mitigation Approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Architecture Drift | Domains diverge from platform-owned templates over time | Enforce shared control templates and periodic conformance checks |
| Security Inconsistency | Identity, authorization, or endpoint-visibility controls implemented unevenly across domains | Centralized identity/policy templates; mandatory architecture and security review gates |
| Operational Gaps | Missing telemetry or runbooks discovered at or after release | Make readiness evidence a mandatory release gate rather than a post-launch afterthought |
| Centralized-Platform Dependency | An outage or misconfiguration in shared gateway, identity, or OTel Collector infrastructure affects every onboarded domain API | Multi-AZ deployment for shared components; documented platform ownership and recovery responsibilities (see Deployment and Operations of the companion [REF-APP-API-001](../../../reference/application/REF-APP-API-001-aws-api-management-reference-architecture.md)) |
